pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2). Recognising odd and even numbers — a first structural property of number, tied to the 2s table and divisibility by 2.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.3 'determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g. by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends'.
• Operational details: define even/odd by the PAIRING test — even = can be split into pairs with none left over (= 2×something); odd = exactly one left unpaired. Connect to the 2s table (even numbers ARE the multiples of 2) and to the ones-digit rule (ends in 0,2,4,6,8 = even). Note 0 is even.
• Checkpoint: classify by structure. Tier A (6): pair up counters and say odd or even for numbers to 10. Tier B (6–7): classify numbers to 20 and state the ones-digit rule. Tier C (7): explain even as 'two equal groups / 2×n' and why 0 is even.
bestPractices: Define odd/even by pairing objects (or making two equal rows), not by memorised endings first — even means everything pairs up with none left over; odd leaves exactly one.
Connect even numbers to the 2s multiplication table and to '2 × something' / two equal addends, so odd/even is understood as a multiplicative/divisibility property, not an arbitrary label.
Derive the ones-digit rule (ends in 0,2,4,6,8) from the pairing pattern rather than teaching it as a bare fact, and apply it to larger numbers.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero objects pair perfectly — none left over) and that odd/even has nothing to do with how big a number is.
Use the hundred square to see even/odd as alternating columns, reinforcing the pattern visually (links to the 2s skip-count pattern).
keyRepresentations: Two equal rows / the 2s array (even = two equal groups)
Ten-frame (full pairs vs one lonely counter)
Hundred square with even numbers shaded (alternating columns)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about a number's SIZE rather than divisibility by 2.
Judging by the first (leading) digit instead of the ones digit.
Believing a number could be both odd and even, or neither.
Not connecting even numbers to the 2s table / '2×n' — treating the ending rule as unrelated to multiplication.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2 / US Grade 2), teach odd and even as a structural property of number: even means a count can be split fully into pairs (or two equal groups) with none left over (= 2×something); odd leaves exactly one unpaired. Build the meaning by pairing physical or on-screen counters, connect it to the 2s table and the ones-digit pattern (ends in 0,2,4,6,8), and make clear that 0 is even and that odd/even has nothing to do with a number's size.

activities.title: Pairing machine: pair the counters and spot the leftover
feedback: When a number pairs cleanly, name it: 'Every counter has a partner — that's EVEN, two equal groups of the same size.'
When one is left over, point to it: 'That single counter with no partner is exactly what ODD means.'
On a ten-frame: 'See the filled pairs — if one cell sits alone with no partner, the number is odd.'
After several tests, highlight the shaded hundred square: 'See how even numbers fall in the same columns and all end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8? That pattern comes from the pairing.'
For 0: 'No counters, so nothing is left over — zero pairs perfectly, so 0 is even.'
If a learner splits 7 into 3 and 4 and calls it even, line the two piles up one-to-one: 'The groups have to match exactly. One counter has no partner, so 7 is odd.'
activities.rationale: Odd/even is defined by the action of pairing, so letting children run the test themselves lets the leftover (the meaning of odd) be seen directly, and lets the digit rule be discovered from the pattern rather than memorised. A ten-frame, an on-screen pairing control with live hundred-square shading, and a two-equal-rows toggle are optional ways to make the pairing mechanism and its link to the 2s table concrete; equivalent work with real counters achieves the same.
sourceClaims: 2.OA.3 determine whether a group (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s; write an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
learnerActions: Choose a quantity of counters (start with numbers to 10, then extend to 20).
Pair the counters up into twos — physically with real counters, or by tapping a 'pair up' control if using a screen model.
Optionally lay the counters on a ten-frame to see full pairs versus one lonely counter.
Decide: if every counter has a partner, the number is EVEN; if exactly one counter is left on its own, the number is ODD.
Test number after number and watch the result build on a hundred square (even numbers shaded) so the alternating-column / ends-in-0,2,4,6,8 pattern appears.
Use a '2×n' / two-equal-rows view to see each even number as two equal groups, linking it to the 2s table.
Test 0: zero counters, zero left over — so 0 is even.
activities.intendedInsight: Even means everything pairs up with none left over (two equal groups / 2×n); odd means exactly one is left unpaired. The ones-digit rule and the 2s table both come from this pairing structure, not from an arbitrary ending.

activities.title: Introduce with a paired vs leftover picture
feedback: Point to the leftover object: 'This one has no partner — that is what makes the set odd.'
On the hundred square: 'The shaded numbers all end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.'
activities.rationale: A fixed image can introduce the paired-vs-leftover contrast and the hundred-square pattern clearly. It cannot be re-run across many different numbers by the learner, so it works best as a first introduction or support alongside hands-on pairing where children test numbers themselves.
learnerActions: Look at a picture that contrasts a set whose objects all pair up (even) with a set that has one object left over (odd).
Tap or point to an even set to reveal its neat pairs; tap an odd set to reveal the single leftover.
Look at a hundred square with even numbers shaded to see the alternating pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: A set that pairs up completely is even; a set with one left over is odd — and even numbers fall in a regular pattern.

activities.title: Sort numbers and check the edge cases
feedback: For 0: 'Zero counters leave nothing over, so 0 is even.'

If a learner uses the first digit (e.g. calls 23 even because of the 2), redirect: 'Look at the ones digit — the tens always pair up, so the ones decide whether one counter is left over. 23 ends in 3, so it is odd.'
For two-digit numbers: 'Tens always pair up, so just check the ones digit.'
activities.rationale: Deliberate edge cases (0, large numbers, a leading-digit distractor) target the common errors that odd/even depends on size or the first digit. A sort can check and practise classification, but it can be answered by the digit rhyme alone without the pairing meaning, so it works best after that meaning is secure and alongside a show-or-explain step.
learnerActions: Sort a mix of numbers (including 0 and two-digit numbers to 20) into 'odd' and 'even' boxes.
Answer: is 0 odd or even? Explain why.
Find the number that breaks a stated rule, and resist a distractor that judges by the leading (first) digit instead of the ones digit.
activities.intendedInsight: The classification holds for every whole number, including0. In base ten, each ten can be paired fully, so the ones digit determines whether a counter remains unpaired; a number’s size or leading digit does not decide its parity.

activities.title: Predict before you pair: does adding one change it?
feedback: Strong reasoning sounds like: 'It will be odd, because the new one has no partner.'
If a learner cannot predict and only reports after counting, revisit pairing: 'Each pair needs two. One extra counter has nobody to pair with, so the total becomes odd.'
Confirm by pairing: '6 made 3 pairs; the 7th counter is left over, so 7 is odd.'
activities.rationale: Asking for the reason before observing distinguishes genuine pairing understanding from reciting the last-digit rule, which is the key diagnostic distinction for this topic.
learnerActions: Start with 6 counters (even). Before touching them, predict whether adding ONE more will keep it even or make it odd — and say why.
Add the counter and pair them up to check your prediction.
Explain the result using pairing: the new counter either finds a partner or is left alone.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding one counter to an even number leaves one unpaired, making it odd; the reason stated before checking shows whether a learner understands pairing or is only reading off a label afterwards.

constraints: Define odd/even by pairing (or making two equal rows) first; introduce the ones-digit rule as something derived from the pairing pattern, not as a bare fact to memorise.
Insist that the two groups be EQUAL and match one-to-one: splitting 7 into 3 and 4 does not make it even. Line the piles up so the unpaired counter is visible.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero counters, none left over) and that odd/even is independent of a number's size.
A paired-vs-leftover picture is an introduction/support: it cannot be run across many numbers by the learner, so pair it with hands-on testing.

A sorting/choice check can teach and check classification but may be answered by the digit rhyme alone; use it after the pairing meaning is secure, and include a show-or-explain step to confirm understanding.
Do not accept the last-digit rule as proof of understanding — ask the learner to show the pairing and explain why one is left over.
Recognition or labelling tasks do not by themselves show that a learner can construct and justify the pairing; include predict-and-explain or show-with-counters tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source asserted that a dialogue 'offers little a talking partner uniquely adds' and that '3D adds nothing' for this planar property; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been dropped rather than propagated. Spoken explanation (e.g. the predict-and-explain task) is in fact used here during teaching.

The original marked an on-screen pairing tool as the uniquely 'ideal' format; this has been softened to an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy of one medium over hands-on counters.

The Y2 DfE curriculum statement ('recognising odd and even numbers' within the 2, 5 and 10 tables) is topic/coverage context only; it has been removed from activity sourceClaims because it asserts no teaching method, and is retained here solely as curriculum context. The 2s-table link remains as design rationale.
One source (CCSS 2.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited because it directly describes the pairing/counting-by-2s method, but its verification is unconfirmed.

Self-audit: pairing arithmetic checked — 8 = 4 pairs (even), 7 = 3 pairs + 1 leftover (odd), 6 = 3 pairs (even), adding 1 to 6 gives 7 (odd), 23 ends in 3 so is odd. The '3 and 4' split of 7 is correctly identified as unequal and therefore NOT evidence of evenness. The leading-digit distractor (e.g. 23 judged by the '2') is corrected to the ones-digit rule in the activity.

assess.poeTask: Give the child 6 counters (even) and ask them to predict, before touching them, whether adding ONE more counter will keep it even or make it odd — and to say why. Then add the counter and pair them up to check. The value is the reason stated before observing: a child who understands pairing predicts 'odd, because the new one has no partner'; a child on the digit-rule alone often cannot predict and only reads off afterwards.
probeDeeper: You paired them up. What does having one left over tell you about 7?
Is 10 odd or even? Can you tell without laying out ten counters?
If I add one more counter to an even pile, does it stay even? Why?
Someone split 7 into 3 and 4 and said it's even. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 7 is odd, 8 is even. A child reasoning correctly pairs the counters up (or splits into two equal groups): 8 makes 4 pairs with none left over, so it is even; 7 makes 3 pairs with one left over, so it is odd — even means it can be shared into two equal groups (or all paired) with nothing left, odd leaves one.

errorPatterns.pattern: decides odd/even by counting-to-say only — knows the last-digit rule but cannot connect it to pairing; thinks 'even' just means 'a number you say when counting by twos'
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT accept the digit rule as proof — have the child pair the counters physically and name 'even = everyone has a partner, odd = one left alone'; connect it back to why the digits work only after the pairing meaning is secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gives the right label but, asked to show it, cannot make the pairs relevant or says 'because it just is / because it ends in 8'

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks a number is even if it can be split into two groups AT ALL, ignoring that the groups must be EQUAL (splits 7 into 3 and 4 and calls it even)
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist the two groups match one-to-one; line the piles up side by side so the leftover in 7 is visibly unpaired.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7 is even (I can make two groups: 3 and 4)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides 7 into two unequal piles and declares it even 'because there are two groups'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes larger numbers are 'more even' or that odd/even alternates unreliably for big numbers — unsure whether e.g. 10 is even because 'it's a big number'
errorPatterns.nextMove: show that only the pairing of the LAST counter matters; group in tens (always even) and check the ones, so the rule scales.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or guesses on two-digit numbers, treating the property as tied to size not structure

responseLevels.gap: labels by rote or guesses; cannot demonstrate with counters; or calls unequal-split numbers even.
responseLevels.full: shows even = full pairing / two equal groups and odd = one left over, explains the leftover as the defining feature, and extends the reasoning to larger numbers via the last digit.
responseLevels.partial: correctly pairs the counters and identifies odd/even for the presented numbers but relies on the last-digit rule for others with no link to pairing — cannot explain why the rule works.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 7 counters. Is 7 odd or even? Now here are 8 counters — is 8 odd or even? For each one, show me with the counters how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Many children label numbers odd/even purely by the last digit rhyme without any idea of WHY. Demanding they SHOW it with counters separates a memorised digit-rule from the pair/equal-share meaning. The child who only knows 'ends in 0,2,4,6,8' cannot demonstrate the leftover, and stumbles on the reason tier.
